canonicalExplanation.summary: Some people get dizzy, nauseous or distracted by motion. When they turn on **Reduce motion** in their OS, browsers expose `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Honour it by **removing large or decorative movement** (parallax, zooming, sliding backgrounds) and replacing essential transitions with **instant or gentle** alternatives like a quick fade — but still show every state change. Also check your experience at **200% zoom** and **keyboard only**.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A course landing page has parallax backgrounds and cards that slide in from the side as you scroll. A learner with a vestibular disorder feels sick within seconds. Their OS has "Reduce motion" on, but the site ignores it. A reduced-motion query removes parallax and uses an instant opacity state change for the same revealed content. In this lesson you'll verify and repair an experience under reduced-motion, zoom and keyboard-only settings.

examples.title: Parallax off, content still revealed
examples.situation: A reduced-motion query removes parallax and uses an instant opacity state change for the same revealed content.
walkthrough: **Removes parallax:** `.hero__bg { transform: none }` inside the query.
**Instant opacity state change:** the card reveal becomes a 1ms fade, so the same revealed content still appears; the browser will render every card, just without sliding.
examples.result: Learners who reduce motion see all the same content and feedback without movement that could make them unwell.

examples.title: The content that never appeared
examples.situation: A global reduce rule sets `animation: none !important` on everything. Cards that start at `opacity: 0` and rely on a fade-in animation now stay invisible.
walkthrough: Removing the animation left the starting state (opacity 0) in place.
Reduced-motion users can't see the cards at all.
Fix: in the reduce query, set the final state directly (`opacity: 1; transform: none`) or use an instant animation.
examples.result: Cards are visible for everyone; only the movement is removed.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Reduced-motion users should receive no state feedback, because every transition must be removed.
misconceptions.correction: Reduced motion asks for less movement, not less information. Remove large or decorative motion, and keep state changes visible through instant or subtle alternatives like a short opacity change.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The content that never appeared", what went wrong with the blanket rule?

analogy.example: Reduced motion is like **turning off a theatre's moving set pieces for an audience member who gets seasick**: the play (content and story) continues; the scenery just stops swinging.
limitations: Theatres can't personalise per seat; browsers can per user.
Some cues (a light change) still help — like a quick fade.

artifact: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .hero__bg { transform: none } .card.reveal { animation: fade-in 1ms both } }

remediation.explanation: For every animation ask: **Is it decorative (remove under reduce) or feedback (make it instant)? What's its final state — is that state still applied when the animation is removed?**

recap.summary: To verify and repair an experience under reduced-motion, zoom and keyboard-only settings, honour prefers-reduced-motion by removing decorative movement and making feedback instant while keeping final states visible, then test at 200% zoom and with the keyboard alone.
